rules.statement: Don't ask for an `OperatingSystem.IsWindows()` guard around `CipherSuitesPolicy` to be narrowed to `OperatingSystem.IsLinux()`. The API works on Linux and macOS and fails only on Windows (SChannel), so `!IsWindows()` is the guard that the `UnsupportedOSPlatform` attribute and the platform analyzer call for.
rules.why: CipherSuitesPolicy is supported on Linux and macOS. A macOS host should get the policy, so narrowing the guard to Linux would wrongly skip it there.
rules.check: Before you report a platform guard as too broad, check the API's `SupportedOSPlatform`/`UnsupportedOSPlatform` attributes. A guard that matches what the platform analyzer asks for is correct.

rules.statement: In a test project, don't ask for a wire-protocol name such as an HTTP header name to be replaced with an internal constant from another assembly that the test project can't see. Also don't suggest adding `InternalsVisibleTo` just to share that constant.
rules.why: Granting InternalsVisibleTo for one constant exposes every internal of the assembly. The name is wire vocabulary, and a test that spells it out also proves the name used on the wire.
rules.check: Before you report a repeated header or parameter literal in a test, check whether the constant is internal to an assembly the test project has no `InternalsVisibleTo` access to.

rules.statement: Don't ask for an id-generator or Guid-provider seam around a single `Guid.NewGuid()` call when the tests already check the generated value's observable properties, such as its canonical format and that it differs from the input.
rules.why: A seam for one call adds an abstraction and a DI registration without making any untested behavior testable.
rules.check: Before you report a direct `Guid.NewGuid()` call, check whether the existing tests already assert the format and uniqueness of the generated value.

rules.statement: When a change alters the security posture that clients or operators can observe (for example a minimum TLS version or restricted cipher suites), add a present-tense entry under `### Security` in the Unreleased section of CHANGELOG.md, and record the decision and its platform limitations in an ADR.
rules.why: Without them, operators see handshake failures they can't explain. The reasoning would otherwise live only in a code comment, where it can drift.
rules.check: Look for changes to TLS protocols, cipher suites or other security settings that come with no `### Security` changelog entry and no ADR.

rules.statement: Put TLS protocol and cipher-suite policy in its own internal type that has unit tests asserting the allowed protocol set, that the suite list holds only AEAD forward-secret suites, and the behavior on each platform. Don't leave it as untested inline configuration.
rules.why: Otherwise a later edit could quietly re-enable TLS 1.0/1.1 or weak suites and no test would catch it.
rules.check: Look for `SslProtocols`, `CipherSuitesPolicy` or `OnAuthenticate` configuration written inline in host setup with no test covering it.

rules.statement: When an endpoint filter promises a behavior on every response (such as echoing a header), test it on a response refused by an earlier filter, such as a 429 from the rate limiter, and not only on a response from the endpoint itself.
rules.why: If the filters were reordered, refused responses could lose the behavior and every test would still pass.
rules.check: Look for tests of a cross-cutting filter that exercise only requests reaching the endpoint handler.

rules.statement: When the same format specifier is used for both parsing and formatting a value (for example a Guid format string), define it once as a private constant and use that constant in both places.
rules.why: If one side changes and the other doesn't, parsing and generation can drift apart.
rules.check: Look for the same bare format-string literal repeated in matching Parse/TryParse and ToString calls.
